title: Is This the World’s Oldest Image of a Mind‑altering Plant?
author: Benjamin Pothier
text:
Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementAnthropologyIs This the World’s Oldest Image of a Mind‑altering Plant?A painted panel deep in a Spanish cave may push the human relationship with mind-altering plants back thousands of years, earlier than anything previously knownBPBy Benjamin Pothier8:30 AM CDT on August 15, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleDeep in the El Castillo cave in northern Spain, up a side passage off the main pathway, there is a small painted panel most visitors would walk straight past.Subscribe to skip adsFeatured VideoCreated some 17,000 to 15,000 years ago, it shows five red signs, each shaped a little like a bell. A natural stone ledge runs beneath them like the lip of an altar. For over a century, archaeologists have simply catalogued these as “bell-shaped signs,” filed under the vast heading of ice age marks we don’t know the meaning of.Building on my Ph.D. research surveying plants used in shamanic ritual worldwide, I argue they may be flowers. Mind-altering flowers, to be specific—the bell of a psychoactive nightshade, most likely belladonna or a local henbane.I published a paper in 2021 making a similar case for a tree drawn on the Chu Silk Manuscript, China’s oldest illustrated text. I read this tree as a plant credited in early Chinese herbals with letting its user see and speak with spirits.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementIf my interpretation is correct, then these unremarkable red signs would be the oldest known picture of a mind-altering plant anywhere in the world, by thousands of years. And it could be corroborated the way it was at Pinwheel Cave in California, where chewed bits of hallucinogenic plant matter found wedged into the rock gave the first unambiguous physical proof anywhere in the world that a plant depicted in rock art had been ingested at the site.Look at a belladonna flower and then at the signs, and the resemblance is hard to unsee: a drooping, five-lobed bell, its mouth flaring outward, with faint veins running down the corolla.The El Castillo signs share this silhouette—the flared bell, the downward hang, and, on several, a central line echoing the vein of the living flower. Henbane, another psychoactive nightshade native to the region, produces a similarly shaped bell at certain stages of its growth.BEAUTIFUL DANGER: Left: A belladonna (Atropa belladonna) flower. Right: Detail of the El Castillo bell signs. Credit: Flower: Flobbadob / Wikimedia Commons | Cave painting photo courtesy of Geneviève Von Petzinger, CC BY.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementSome might argue that a bell is a simple form, and simple forms recur by chance. But what I feel lifts these signs above coincidence is the company they keep: the deliberate grouping, the altar-like ledge, and the weight of independent evidence that prehistoric Europeans knew these plants intimately.Other readings exist. Following the French archaeologist André Leroi-Gourhan’s mid 20th-century framework, ovals, triangles, and rounded forms across Palaeolithic sites like these bell-shaped signs were often catalogued as vulvar or female symbols. Some specialists, including Canadian paleoanthropologist Genevieve von Petzinger, have since pushed back on this once-dominant interpretive lens. They argue that it reflects the assumptions of the—largely male—early researchers, as much as the evidence itself.A plant Europe never forgotThe nightshades are among the most written-about psychoactive plants in European history. Their active compounds—atropine, scopolamine, hyoscyamine—produce vivid hallucinations and the striking sensation that one’s skin is sprouting fur or feathers.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementANCIENT SCULPTURE: The lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel. Credit: Dagmar Hollmann, CC BY.This has echoes of the part-human, part-animal figures common in ice age art, from the lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel—a 40,000-year-old ivory carving with a human body and the head of a cave lion—and the “sorcerers” of French caves, human figures fused with antlers, claws, or a beast’s tail, long read as shamans caught mid-transformation.There is also evidence that these plants were used in rituals by later Europeans. Chemical analysis of Bronze Age human hair from the burial cave of Es Càrritx in Menorca confirms people there consumed multiple psychoactive compounds, atropine and scopolamine among them, around 3,000 years ago.Belladonna’s use threads through European history right up to the witch trials in Germany, France and Italy, roughly from the 15th to 17th centuries, where it was considered a staple of the “flying ointments” said to carry witches to the sabbath. The question this panel poses is how far back that thread runs.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementThe documented relationship between humans and mind-altering plants, in image form, essentially begins in the neolithic. The famous “mushroom” figures of Tassili n'Ajjer in the Sahara—a vast Algerian plateau of prehistoric art, where humanoid figures appear studded with mushroom-like shapes—have been read by some researchers as an early depiction of ritual mushroom use. The oldest widely discussed candidates date to roughly 7,000 to 9,000 years ago.The El Castillo panel belongs, according to a chronological study of the cave’s iconographic stratigraphy (overlapping layers of cave art), to the lower Magdalenian Period—some 17,000 to 15,000 years ago, deep in the last ice age. That would push the picture back 7,000 to 10,000 years, into the upper Palaeolithic.CAVE ART: Inside the main room of the El Castillo Cave. Credit: Government of Cantabria Press Office, CC BY-SAIt’s a large leap, and one that opens a long gap in the record that is reason for caution: A 2023 survey of 5,786 catalogued images across 113 European Palaeolithic caves found that plants account for just 0.07 percent of them, against over half for animals. This near-absence that may reflect how little we have looked for plants, and how easily a painted flower gets filed away as an abstract sign.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementDirectly beneath the panel sits a shrine-like stone concretion—exactly the kind of surface on which offerings might have been placed. This would not be unprecedented: At Chauvet Cave in southeastern France, a cave bear skull was deliberately placed on a flat stone block, with traces of a fire lit beneath it, in what excavators have described as an altar-like arrangement roughly 36,000 years old. Modern techniques for recovering ancient environmental DNA from sediment are sensitive enough that traces of Solanaceae—the nightshade family, which includes belladonna and henbane—could support the reading.That testability is why the claim is worth putting before a wider audience now. If wrong, a field study will show it. If right, it would mean the human impulse to make images and the human use of mind-altering plants are entangled at the very origin of art.
